newsitem.title: USA: Sprint results higher, but hurt by charges, costs.
newsitem.headline: Sprint results higher, but hurt by charges, costs.

text.p: Sprint Corp. Tuesday reported strong fourth-quarter and 1996 profits, as consumers boosted long-distance usage and added more phone lines for faxes and Internet access.

But profits at the nation's second largest long-distance company were eroded by slightly higher-than-expected charges and start-up costs for its Global One joint venture and Sprint PCS, its wireless phone venture.
Sprint said it earned $245.3 million, or 57 cents a share, in the quarter, including a $60 million charge related to litigation involving its long-distance division.
In the year-ago period, Sprint lost $343.2 million, or 98 cents a share, after the local phone division recorded an $88 million restructuring charge.
Revenues edged up to $3.6 billion from $3.3 billion.
Fourth quarter operating earnings, excluding charges and venture expenses, rose to $347 million from $290 million.
For the full year, net profits almost tripled to $1.18 billion from $395.3 million. Revenues rose to $14.0 billion from $12.8 billion.
Analysts said the losses from ventures were higher than expected, pushing net earnings a few cents a share short of average estimates for the quarter.
"It continues to show strong core growth offset by increased dilution from new ventures," said Simon Flannery, an analyst at J.P. Morgan.

For the quarter, Sprint PCS cut the company's earnings by $71.4 million versus $18.9 million the previous year. Sprint has a 40 percent stake in the wireless Personal Communications Services ventuer. Its partners include Tele-Communications Inc., Cox Communications and Comcast Corp.
Global One, owned by Sprint, Deutsche Telekom AG and France Telecom, cost Sprint $30.6 million for the quarter compared with $11.9 million in the 1995 quarter.
Sprint said it expects earnings per share to decline in 1997 due to increased investment, but the company said it was bullish about its prospects.
"The start-up costs (of PCS) will cause pressure on earnings, and those will actually peak in 1998," Ronald LeMay, president and chief operating officer, said in an interview.
He said the company is confident in the long-term PCS business and considers it "strategic" to Sprint.
Analysts seemed to agree.
"The bottom line is that by mid-year, Sprint is going to trade on the subscriber growth in PCS," said Michael Elling at Prudential Securities.
Sprint's long-distance revenues rose 12.3 percent to $2.16 billion in the quarter while operating income jumped 27.4 percent to $257 million.
Minutes of long-distance use rose 21 percent from the fourth quarter 1995.
Local telephone revenues grew 7.9 percent in the fourth quarter to $1.33 billion and operating income rose 12.4 percent to $334 million, Sprint said.

Access lines grew 5.6 percent in the quarter to more than 7.1 million, Sprint said. The company said nearly a third of the added lines were for second-line service to existing customers for Internet access or fax machines, for example.
Chief financial officer Arthur Krause said the company expects profit growth of its core long-distance business in the double digits in the first quarter and all of 1997.
"We currently see no impediments to this momentum and we are targeting double-digit volume and revenue growth for the full year of 1997," Krause said.
He said, however, that first-quarter volume growth may slow slightly due in part to the lack of toll-free lines for the Internal Revenue Service, which in the past had a strong seasonal impact.
Overall, Sprint said the continued expenses will pay off.
"Irrespective of this near-term earnings trend, we are very bullish about our prospects," Krause said.
Sprint stock rose 75 cents to $41 on the New York Stock Exchange.
